passages.t: Rest for Jacob, and a taunt over the king of Babylon
passages.happening:
‘For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land’ (verse 1). Foreigners will join them. The nations will bring Israel home, and those who took them captive will become their captives (verse 2).

‘On the day that the LORD gives you rest from your pain and torment, and from the hard labor into which you were forced’ (verse 3), they will sing a song of contempt against the king of Babylon: ‘How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended’ (verse 4). The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, which struck the peoples with unceasing blows (verses 5-6). ‘All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song’ (verse 7). Even the cedars of Lebanon rejoice, since no woodcutter comes against them now (verse 8).

Sheol stirs the spirits of the dead to meet him, all the kings of the earth (verse 9). They say, ‘You too have become weak, as we are’ (verse 10). His pomp has gone down to Sheol. ‘Maggots are your bed and worms your blanket’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 13 announced Babylon's overthrow. Chapter 14 tells what it will mean for God's people: return, rest and a song. The forced labor of verse 3 recalls Egypt. The exodus will happen again.

The taunt song is one of the great poems of the Bible. The king of Babylon is not named, and scholars have proposed several candidates. Some think of the Assyrian king Sargon II, who also ruled Babylon and died in battle in 705 BC, his body apparently never recovered. Others think of Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar or Nabonidus. Many read the poem as a portrait of the imperial tyrant as such, applied to the king of Babylon because Babylon came to stand for the empire that exiled Judah.

Sheol is the realm of the dead, pictured as a shadowy place where the dead kings sit on their thrones. They rise to greet the newcomer with scorn, telling him he is as weak as they are now. The cedars of Lebanon rejoice because the emperors who cut them for their palaces are gone.

Verse 2's picture of captors made captive is the language of reversal in an age of empires. It describes what the oppressed hoped for. It gives no one a warrant to rule over any people now.
passages.later: Revelation sings a similar song over the fall of a later Babylon, the proud city of its own day (Revelation 18). And Ezekiel pictures ‘Mighty chiefs’ speaking ‘from the midst of Sheol’ about a fallen empire (Ezekiel 32:21).
passages.asks: The whole earth breaks into song when the oppressor falls. Ask what oppression in the world you long to see end. And ask whether your rest depends on someone else's power, or on God's.

passages.t: How you have fallen, O day star
passages.happening:
“How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations” (verse 12).

He said in his heart that he would ascend to heaven and raise his throne above the stars of God, and sit on the mount of assembly in the far north (verse 13). ‘I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High’ (verse 14). ‘But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit’ (verse 15).

Those who see him will stare: is this the man who shook the earth, turned the world into a desert, and would not let his captives go home (verses 16-17)? The kings of the nations lie in their tombs, but he is thrown out of his grave like a rejected branch (verses 18-19). He will not be buried with them, because he destroyed his own land and people (verse 20). His line will end (verse 21). The LORD will cut off Babylon's name and sweep her away ‘with the broom of destruction’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The tyrant's boast uses pictures from the religious stories of his world. The day star, the morning star, rises bright and is soon lost in the sun. The mount of assembly in the far north was where the gods were thought to meet. The king wanted to climb above them all and make himself like the Most High. Instead he goes down to the lowest pit.

To be left unburied was the worst disgrace in the ancient world. Kings built great tombs for themselves. This king is denied one.

Verse 21 speaks of the tyrant's sons being killed for their fathers' sins, so that his dynasty will not rise again. It is the language of a ruling family's end in the wars of that age. Israel's own law and prophets said that children are not to be put to death for their parents' sins, and the verse is no warrant for harming anyone's children.
passages.later: Ezekiel describes the king of Tyre in similar terms: ‘Your heart grew proud of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor; so I cast you to the earth’ (Ezekiel 28:17). Jesus said, ‘everyone who exalts himself will be humbled’ (Luke 14:11).
passages.hard:
Is Isaiah 14:12 about the fall of Satan?

The text itself says it is a taunt against the king of Babylon (verse 4), and verse 16 calls him a man. Most modern interpreters, including many conservative ones, read verses 12 to 15 first as a portrait of a human tyrant, described with images from the religious stories of the day.

From the early centuries of the church, many Christian writers also read the passage as describing the fall of Satan, whose pride they saw as the pattern behind every proud ruler. The Latin rendering of day star, lucifer, attached that name to him. Some readers today hold a double reference: the human king is the subject, but his boast mirrors a spiritual rebellion behind him, as Ezekiel 28 describes the king of Tyre in similar terms. Others think that reading goes beyond what the text supports.

These notes take no side. The passage does not give a detailed account of Satan's origin either way, and its main point stands on every reading: pride that reaches for God's throne ends in the Pit.
passages.asks: The tyrant said in his heart that he would ‘make myself like the Most High’ (verse 14). Ask where that thought hides in your own heart, in smaller forms. And ask what it would mean to stop climbing.

passages.t: God's oath against Assyria, and a word to Philistia
passages.happening:
The LORD of Hosts has sworn: ‘Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand’ (verse 24). He will break Assyria in his land and trample him on his mountain, and take Assyria's yoke off his people (verse 25). ‘This is the plan devised for the whole earth’ (verse 26). ‘The LORD of Hosts has purposed, and who can thwart Him?’ (verse 27).

‘In the year that King Ahaz died, this burden was received’ (verse 28). ‘Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken. For a viper will spring from the root of the snake’ (verse 29). The poor will find pasture and the needy lie down in safety, but Philistia's root will die (verse 30). A cloud of smoke comes from the north (verse 31).

What answer will be given to the envoys of that nation? ‘The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The chapter runs from the far future (Babylon) to the near future (Assyria) to the present moment (the year Ahaz died). The same purpose of God stands over all three.

Assyria dominated Judah throughout Isaiah's ministry. The promise to break it in God's own land and on his mountain fits the events of 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army besieged Jerusalem and withdrew.

The year Ahaz died is itself disputed: about 727 BC on one reckoning, about 715 BC on another. The broken rod that had struck Philistia may be an Assyrian king who had recently died, such as Tiglath-pileser III, who died in 727 BC and whose campaigns had crushed the Philistine cities; some take it as another ruler. The Philistines, who held Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath, repeatedly rebelled against Assyria and looked for allies. Verse 32 pictures their envoys in Jerusalem seeking Judah's support. Isaiah's answer is that Zion's safety is in the LORD, not in alliances.
passages.later: The oath was kept when ‘the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (Isaiah 37:36). A psalm says the same of God's plans: ‘The counsel of the LORD stands forever’ (Psalm 33:11).
passages.asks: God says his plan stands and asks who can thwart him. Ask which of your own plans you hold more tightly than his. And ask where you go for refuge when the envoys come asking you to join their alliance.
